newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Scientists scour oceans for new medicines.
newsitem.headline: Scientists scour oceans for new medicines.

text.p: Nearly a thousand feet (300 metres) below the surface of the blue-green Bahamian waters, a research submarine plumbs the murky deep for sea plants that might hold a cure for allergies, Alzheimer's, arthritis, cancer or AIDS.

Its powerful searchlight focused on a barren wall powdered with snowy sediment, the hi-tech submersible inches upward as researchers strain for a glimpse of a brightly coloured sponge, a waving sea fan or a minute, dark-green doughnut of algae.

At 470 feet (143 metres), the sub hovers as its robot arm reaches out. A powerful suction tube slurps up the target, a small whitish sponge with tubes like chimneys. Pieces zip through the plastic tube into a bucket on the front of the sub.
"This could be it. Could be the cure," said Dr. Amy Wright, a marine chemist with the Harbour Branch Oceanographic Institution, a leading U.S. ocean research group.

Marine scientists are going to spectacular lengths -- and depths -- to find cures for what ails humankind. The deep-sea prospectors search for algae, sponges and other organisms that produce unique chemical compounds found nowhere else on Earth.

Buoyed by increasingly sophisticated technology that has allowed them to explore where wading, snorkeling or scuba (self-contained underwater breathing apparatus) never could, the prospectors are exploring ever more remote corners of the oceans, which they suspect -- or hope -- will take them far beyond time-tested cod liver oil to a vast array of remedies for ailments ranging from cancer to obesity and hair loss.

"Nature is very creative in coming up with chemical syntheses and designing enzymes that will do certain things," Wright said. "Nature has already done the biotesting for us. We just need to figure out what it will do in our systems."

From their base in Fort Pierce, Florida, Harbour Branch scientists have searched the waters of the Caribbean, the Galapagos, the Canary Islands, the Azores, Australia and other far-flung locales for unusual chemical compounds.

Medical science has long sought radical remedies in the world's rainforests. Yet biomedical exploration of the oceans, which cover 70 percent of the Earth's surface, is in its infancy. Scientists have catalogued perhaps 10,000 marine organisms, the barest fraction of what may lie in the depths.

"We've just scratched the surface," said Dr. Shirley Pomponi, director of Biomedical Research at Harbour Branch. "We think that we've probably got less than one percent of the marine microorganisms that there are out there."

Already scientists have isolated from sea creatures a series of compounds called topsentins that may become a treatment for arthritis and a chemical called discodermolide that works against breast and ovarian cancer. They are working on mass production of a compound that kills melanoma cells.

Aboard Harbour Branch's Johnson-Sea-Link, a four-person sub capable of reaching depths of 3,000 feet (914 metres), searchers pause at a point about 450 feet (137 metres) beneath the surface near a deep-water cleft called "Tongue of the Ocean," not far from where Disney's "20,000 Leagues Under the Sea" was filmed.

A bright yellow sponge, perhaps two inches (five cms) in length, stands out in stark contrast to the crusty gray of the wall. "We call that one yellow frilly," said Wright, watching the wall on a video screen in the sub's rear compartment. "That's an interesting sponge."

Encased in a sphere of plastic 5 1/4 inches (13 cms) thick as protection from crushing pressure, the sub's pilot videotapes and photographs the sample before using the suction tube to vacuum the specimen into a bucket.

The prospectors collect meticulously, perhaps a dozen samples on each dive. Sometimes it is a sponge or algae familiar to them and known to contain a promising compound. Other times they run across a specimen never seen before.
They document the location of each find in case the sample contains the blockbuster cure. "You always hope," Wright said. "You just don't know."
"What makes it pretty interesting is that each one of those organisms potentially could have a unique chemical compound that may have therapeutic value," Pomponi said.
